lesson.subtitle: Lesson 16 -- The Global Presentation
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Renato Annunciato | Lesson 16 -- The Global Presentation

listenings.text: Hi Renato, it is Claire. A few notes before your presentation next week. You have fifteen minutes, so please talk for twelve and leave three for questions. Last year, two managers ran over, and we had no time for questions, which is the part I care about most. Start with a hook, not with the agenda. My team will be on the call from four countries, and some of them are not native speakers either, so a slower pace is a gift, not a weakness. Pause after every number, because people need two seconds to write it down. Do not read your slides. I would rather see you look at the camera with a cue card in your hand. And please prepare for three hard questions: the drop in the South, the recovery plan, and what you need from us. If you finish with one clear request, I can usually say yes on the same call. Good luck. I am looking forward to it.

The first time I presented to the global team in English, I was so nervous that I finished a twenty-minute presentation in eleven minutes. I rushed every slide. My director told me later that nobody understood my numbers, because I said them too fast. My nerves also produced filler words. I said so, and, um, maybe forty times. For the second presentation, I changed three things. First, I did the rehearsal out loud, five times, standing up, with a timer. Second, I wrote my opening and my closing line on a cue card, word for word, because those are the moments when the nerves are worst. Third, I recorded myself and counted my filler words. The number went down from forty to six. My body language changed too. I stopped holding the table. The presentation was not perfect, but at the end the vice president asked me two questions, and that is how I knew they were really listening.

extra_audio.text: Good morning, and thank you for your time. Last year, my team grew market share by three percentage points. Today I will walk you through our results, one problem, and our plan. To close, I will ask you for one thing.

reading.rtitle: Rehearsing for a Senior Audience -- Notes from the Academy
paras: A presentation to a senior audience is won or lost before the meeting starts, in the rehearsal. Reading your slides in silence is not a rehearsal. A real rehearsal is out loud, standing up, with a timer, and if possible with one colleague who asks hard questions.
Plan to talk for about eighty percent of your time. If you have fifteen minutes, prepare twelve. Most presenters run over because they add details on the day, not because they planned too much.

Most of your message is in your delivery. Speak at a slower pace than feels natural, pause after every important number, and keep eye contact with the camera or the room. Filler words are normal, but if you count more than ten in one minute, practice that part again.

Finally, write two sentences word for word: your opening and your closing line. Everything else can be key words on a cue card. Nerves are strongest at the beginning and at the end, and a sentence you know by heart will carry you through.
